Perturbative global solutions of a large class of cross diffusion systems in any dimension

Abstract

This article focuses on a large family of cross-diffusion systems of the form ∂tU−Δ​A​(U)=0\partial_{t}U-\Delta A(U)=0, in dimension d∈𝐍∗d\in\mathbf{N}^{*}, and where U∈𝐑2U\in\mathbf{R}^{2}. We show that under natural conditions on the nonlinearity AA, those systems have a unique smooth (nonnegative for all components) solution when the initial data are small enough in a suitable norm.

1 Introduction

Cross diffusion systems constitute a large class of systems of PDEs which naturally appear in physics as well as population dynamics (see for instance [16, Chapter 4] for several examples). The term cross diffusion is used when in a system of parabolic PDEs, at least one of the diffusion rates in the equation for one component depends on the value of one or more of the other components.

We focus here on the case when the system can be written under the form

{∂tu−Δ⁡[(d1+p⁡(u,v))​u]=0,∂tv−Δ⁡[(d2+q⁡(u,v))​v]=0,\left\{\begin{lgathered}\partial_{t}u-\Delta\big[(d_{1}+p(u,v))u\big]=0,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta\big[(d_{2}+q(u,v))v\big]=0,\end{lgathered}\right. (1)

where d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0 are two constants, and p,qp,q are two elements of 𝐑+​[X,Y]\mathbf{R}_{+}[X,Y] (polynomials of two variables with real nonnegative coefficients) vanishing at (0,0)(0,0), and we consider periodic boundary conditions, that is the system is considered on the torus 𝐓d\mathbf{T}^{d}. It can be checked, at least formally, that a solution of these systems remain nonnegative for all t≥0t\geq 0 whenever it is initially nonnegative. In the sequel of this paper, we systematically denote U:=(u,v)U:=(u,v).

Note that the classical Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto (called SKT in the rest of the paper) system (see [27]), where pp and qq are linear w.r.t u,vu,v, enters in this category (if the zero-th order competition terms are dropped). Many natural extensions of this system where p,qp,q are not linear any more also enter this category.

Before stating our main theorems, let us fix a (rather weak) setting for which each equation of (1) is well-posed. For this purpose, we rely on the following result.

Lemma 1.

Consider μ∈Lloc∞​(𝐑+,L∞​(𝐓d))\mu\in\textnormal{L}_{\textnormal{loc}}^{\infty}(\mathbf{R}_{+};\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d})) such that infμ>0\inf\mu>0, zin∈H−1​(𝐓d)z_{\textnormal{in}}\in\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}), and f∈Lloc2​(𝐑+,L2​(𝐓d))f\in\textnormal{L}_{\textnormal{loc}}^{2}(\mathbf{R}_{+};\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbf{T}^{d})). Then, there exists a unique z∈Lloc2​(𝐑+,L2​(𝐓d))z\in\textnormal{L}_{\textnormal{loc}}^{2}(\mathbf{R}_{+};\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbf{T}^{d})) such that, after extending all functions by 00 on 𝐑−×𝐓d\mathbf{R}_{-}\times\mathbf{T}^{d}, the following holds (δ0\delta_{0} is the Dirac mass at point 00 on 𝐑\mathbf{R})

∂tz−Δ⁡(μ​z)=Δ​f+δ0⊗zin, in ​𝒟′​(𝐑×𝐓d).\displaystyle\partial_{t}z-\Delta(\mu z)=\Delta f+\delta_{0}\otimes z_{\textnormal{in}},\text{ in }\mathscr{D}^{\prime}(\mathbf{R}\times\mathbf{T}^{d}).

Furthermore, this solution zz belongs to 𝒞⁡([0,T],H−1​(𝐓d))\mathscr{C}([0,T];\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})) and satisfies the following estimate for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]:

‖z⁡(t,⋅)‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+∫0t∫𝐓dμ​z2≤‖zi​n‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+(∫𝐓dzi​n)2​∫0t∫𝐓dμ+∫0t∫𝐓df2μ.\|z(t,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\mu\,z^{2}\\ \leq\|z_{in}\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\left(\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}z_{in}\right)^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\mu+\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\frac{f^{2}}{\mu}. (2)
Proof.

See [4, Lemma 1] (for the estimate) and [23, Theorem 3] (for the well-posedness). ∎

It may be readily checked that for nonnegative bounded densities u,vu,v, each equation of (1) is a particular case of the Kolmogorov equation considered in Lemma 1, in the case of a vanishing source term f=0f=0. Estimate (2) is a generalization of the celebrated duality estimate (see [24] for the seminal version and [18] for a similar one). The case f≠0f\neq 0 will be used crucially in our stability result Theorem 2 below, generalizing the analysis done in [4] for the classical SKT system.

Definition 1.

In the well-posedness setting of Lemma 1, we speak of dual solution. We use the same naming for solutions (u,v)(u,v) of (1) that match this setting for each equation.

We now write down the main results of this paper (Theorems 1 and 2), respectively related to existence and stability/uniqueness of solutions to system (1). We need for that to define the following norm.

Definition 2.

For k∈[1,∞]k\in[1,\infty], and φ∈𝒞∞​(𝐓d)\varphi\in\mathscr{C}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d}), let

Nk​(φ):=(∫0+∞‖et​Δ​φ‖kk​𝑑t)1/k.\displaystyle N_{k}(\varphi):=\left(\int_{0}^{+\infty}\|e^{t\Delta}\varphi\|_{k}^{k}\,\mathrm{d}t\right)^{1/k}.

Remark 1.

This choice of notation Bk​(𝐓d)\textnormal{B}_{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) for the completion is here to remind the reader that such a norm is common in the study of Besov spaces. Actually, this norm is equivalent to the one which usually defines B˙k,k−2/k(𝐓d)\dot{\textnormal{B}}_{k,k}^{-2/k}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) (see for instance [3, Theorem 2.34] for the euclidean setting). It can be directly checked here that in the case when k=2k=2, the norm NkN_{k} is equivalent to the H−1​(𝐓d)\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) norm.

Theorem 1.

Let d∈𝐍∗d\in\mathbf{N}^{*}, d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0 be two constants, and p,qp,q be two elements of 𝐑+​[X,Y]\mathbf{R}_{+}[X,Y] vanishing at (0,0)(0,0). We also consider k>1+d2k>1+\frac{d}{2}.

Then there exists a constant δ>0\delta>0 (depending on dd, d1,d2,p,qd_{1},d_{2},p,q and kk) such that for nonnegative initial data uin,vin∈L∞​(𝐓d)∩H−1​(𝐓d)u_{\mathrm{in}},v_{\mathrm{in}}\in\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d})\cap\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) satisfying

and

‖u⁡(t)−∫𝐓duin‖2+‖v⁡(t)−∫𝐓dvin‖2​⟶t→+∞ 0,\displaystyle\left\|u(t)-\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}u_{\mathrm{in}}\right\|_{2}+\left\|v(t)-\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}v_{\mathrm{in}}\right\|_{2}\,\operatorname*{\longrightarrow}_{t\rightarrow+\infty}\,0, (3)

with an exponential rate.

Theorem 2.

Let d∈𝐍∗d\in\mathbf{N}^{*}, d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0 be two constants, and p,qp,q be two elements of 𝐑+​[X,Y]\mathbf{R}_{+}[X,Y] vanishing at (0,0)(0,0). Then there exist two constants δ,C>0\delta,\textnormal{C}>0 depending on dd, d1,d2,p,qd_{1},d_{2},p,q such that (when T>0T>0) for any pair (u1,v1)(u_{1},v_{1}) and (u2,v2)(u_{2},v_{2}) of L∞​([0,T],L∞​(𝐓d))∩𝒞0​([0,T],H−1​(𝐓d))\textnormal{L}^{\infty}([0,T];\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d}))\cap\mathscr{C}^{0}([0,T];\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})) nonnegative dual solutions to system (1) in the sense of Definition 1 which are such that (for i=1,2i=1,2)

ess​supt∈[0,T]⁡(‖ui​(t)‖∞+‖vi​(t)‖∞)≤δ,\esssup_{t\in[0,T]}\bigg(\|u_{i}(t)\|_{\infty}+\|v_{i}(t)\|_{\infty}\bigg)\leq\delta,

the following stability estimate for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] holds:

∥(u1−u2)(t)||H−1​(𝐓d)+∥(v1−v2)(t)||H−1​(𝐓d)≤‖(u1−u2)​(0)‖H−1​(𝐓d)+‖(v1−v2)​(0)‖H−1​(𝐓d)+C​T​(|∫𝐓d(u1−u2)​(0)|+|∫𝐓d(v1−v2)​(0)|).\|(u_{1}-u_{2})(t)||_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}+\|(v_{1}-v_{2})(t)||_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}\\ \leq||(u_{1}-u_{2})(0)||_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}+||(v_{1}-v_{2})(0)||_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}\\ +\,\textnormal{C}\,T\,\bigg(\bigg|\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}(u_{1}-u_{2})(0)\bigg|+\bigg|\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}(v_{1}-v_{2})(0)\bigg|\bigg).
Remark 2.

We have chosen a simple formulation for Theorem 2, in which both solutions are small in L∞\textnormal{L}^{\infty}, for the sake of clarity. However, our method actually proves a finer statement in which only one of the two solutions has to be small (the other one being given), see Proposition 1.

Combining Theorem 2 with Theorem 1, we infer the following corollary of well-posedness for the system.

Corollary 1.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1, if δ\delta is chosen sufficiently small, the solutions given in Theorem 1 satisfy the stability estimate of Theorem 2. In particular, such solutions are unique (among those satisfying the assumptions required in Theorem 2).

SKT-like systems have been studied for a long time. As they were originally introduced in [27] for the emergence of patterns formation, the first articles focused on their stationary solutions, see [21, 22, 28] for instance. Existence of solutions for these systems has been the source of a large literature which interestingly enough only started 5 years after the publication of [27]. Indeed, the first existence result seems to be the one of Kim in [17], which established that there are global (strong) solutions but only for equal diffusion rates, in dimension 11. After several partial results of this kind, an important step was made by Amann [1, 2], paving the way for a systematic local existence theory (with a blowup criterion) under a mild elliptic condition on the system (also known as « normal ellipticity », that is Petrovskii’s condition for parabolic systems). In the wake of Amann’s theory, a substantial number of articles attempted to prove the existence of global strong solutions of SKT-like systems through a uniform control of Amann’s blowup criterion, generally at the price of restrictive constraints on the system. For instance, in the so-called triangular case, that is when cross diffusion is present only in one of the two equations of the system, Lou, Ni and Wu obtained existence and regularity in dimension 22 in [20], whereas later Choi, Lui and Yamada first got rid of the restriction on the dimension in [26], at the price of considering small cross diffusion rates. More recently, [14] established the existence of global smooth solutions for triangular SKT-like systems when some self diffusion is present, and [13] proved the same kind of results for natural extensions of triangular SKT-like systems.

In the general (non triangular) case, global weak solutions of the SKT system were proven to exist in full generality in [6] ; a few years later [9, 10], similar global solutions were built for some systems having a structure like (1), with possibly non-polynomial diffusion rates (see also [19, 7, 8] for multi-species cases). One common aspect of all these works is that one assumes the existence of an entropy structure for the studied system, which gives rise to a convex Lyapunov functional. Its dissipation allows a control of the gradients of the solutions.

Be it for local, global, weak or strong solutions, in all the previous results, the considered systems always satisfy the normal ellipticity condition. Articles dealing with parabolic systems potentially failing to satisfy this condition are less frequent in the literature (see [12, 29] for recent examples). In a perturbative setting, it was first noticed in [5] (in dimension 11), that one can obtain global strong solutions, when the initial data are small. There, the very same energy estimate that one wishes to obtain thanks to some uniform bound can precisely be used to prove those uniform bounds ; this is due to the embedding H1​(𝐓)↪L∞​(𝐓)\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbf{T})\hookrightarrow\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}) and it allows to prove Theorem 2.1 in [5] that we reproduce here in the specific case of (conservative) system (1) for the sake of clarity (we use the notation ≲\lesssim for “less than a constant times” here and in the rest of the paper).

Theorem 3.

(consequence of [5, Theorem 2.1]) In dimension d=1d=1, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that, for any smooth initial data Uin:=(uin,vin)U_{\mathrm{in}}:=(u_{\mathrm{in}},v_{\mathrm{in}}) satisfying ‖Uin‖∞+‖∇Uin‖2≤δ\|U_{\mathrm{in}}\|_{\infty}+\|\nabla U_{\mathrm{in}}\|_{2}\leq\delta, any smooth solution U:=(u,v)U:=(u,v) to system (1) defined on 𝐑+×𝐓d\mathbf{R}_{+}\times\mathbf{T}^{d} (initialized by Ui​nU_{in}) satisfies

supt≥0‖U⁡(t)‖∞≲δ,supt≥0‖∇U​(t)‖2≲δ.\displaystyle\sup_{t\geq 0}\|U(t)\|_{\infty}\lesssim\delta,\qquad\sup_{t\geq 0}\|\nabla U(t)\|_{2}\lesssim\delta.
Remark 3.

This estimate allows to build global uniformly bounded solutions for all times, after introducing an adequate approximate scheme.

Note that our Theorem 1 can be seen as an extension of Theorem 3 in the case of dimension d≥1d\geq 1, since it is possible to take k=2k=2 when d=1d=1, so that the norms used in the two theorems become equivalent.

We explain here how our result could probably be generalized.

  • —

    First, the fact that p,qp,q are polynomials vanishing at point (0,0)(0,0) with nonnegative coefficients is not essential to our analysis (though it helps greatly in the presentation of the results). It is indeed sufficient to suppose that p,qp,q are nonnegative functions of class 𝒞1​((𝐑+)2)\mathscr{C}^{1}((\mathbf{R}_{+})^{2}) which vanish at point (0,0)(0,0) (note that the explicit estimate of stability has then to be slightly changed).

  • —

    Secondly, we think that our analysis could be reproduced, without much change, when systems of more than two equations are considered (in this direction, see for instance [8] for the existence of global weak solutions for multi-species system).

  • —

    Finally, we insist that our methods cannot work (at least when one looks for global in time solutions) if reaction terms are introduced in the cross diffusion systems, except in very specific cases. For example, if one considers competition terms of Lotka-Volterra type (such as they naturally appear in SKT-type models), one cannot hope to have solutions which remain small when the time becomes large, except if the coefficients appearing in the competition terms are such that associated steady solutions are themselves small. We however think that our result can be extended in at least one general situation, namely when the reaction terms are respectively of the form −u​s1​(u,v)-u\,s_{1}(u,v), −v​s2​(u,v)-v\,s_{2}(u,v), where s1,s2∈𝐑+​[X,Y]s_{1},s_{2}\in\mathbf{R}_{+}[X,Y]. Such a form can correspond for example, in terms of modeling, to situations in population dynamics in which no new individuals are introduced (no births).

In section 2, we present the main a priori estimate underlying the proof of Theorem 1, while we rigorously prove this Theorem in section 3. Then, the proof of Theorem 2 is written is section 4, and some counterexamples are presented in section 5. Finally, Appendices A, B and C summarize some classical results (mainly from the theory of parabolic PDEs), while Appendix D is dedicated to the presentation of an alternative to the a priori estimate of section 2.

2 Global uniform a priori estimates for small initial data

In this section, we write down the a priori estimate which enables to show the existence result (that is, Theorem 1). We recall Definition 2 of the NkN_{k} norm, for k∈[1,∞]k\in[1,\infty], and write down the

Proposition 1.

Let d∈𝐍∗d\in\mathbf{N}^{*}, d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0 be two constants, and p,qp,q be two elements of 𝐑+​[X,Y]\mathbf{R}_{+}[X,Y] vanishing at (0,0)(0,0). We also consider k>1+d2k>1+\frac{d}{2}.

4 Proof of the stability and uniqueness theorem

In this section, we prove Theorem 2. This result is reminiscent of the stability estimate derived in [4, Theorem 1] and is more precisely a consequence of Lemma 1. This stability estimate applies for bounded solutions of the system if one of them is small enough. It is a consequence of the more precise Proposition 2 below. In order to write it down, we introduce for R>0R>0 the cone CR+\textnormal{C}^{+}_{R} containing all nonnegative elements of the L∞​(𝐑+,𝐓d)2\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{R}_{+};\mathbf{T}^{d})^{2} ball of size RR, and LR\textnormal{L}_{R} a common Lipschitz constant for both pp and qq on the compact set {(u,v)∈𝐑2:max⁡(|u|,|v|)≤R}\{(u,v)\in\mathbf{R}^{2}\,:\,\max(|u|,|v|)\leq R\}.

Proof.

The definition of LRL_{R} ensures that for any pair (uk,vk)(u_{k},v_{k}), k=1,2k=1,2, one has

max⁡(|p⁡(u1,v1)−p⁡(u2,v2)|2,|q⁡(u1,v1)−q⁡(u2,v2)|2)≤LR2​(|u1−u2|2+|v1−v2|2)\max\Big(|p(u_{1},v_{1})-p(u_{2},v_{2})|^{2},|q(u_{1},v_{1})-q(u_{2},v_{2})|^{2}\Big)\leq\textnormal{L}_{R}^{2}\,\big(|u_{1}-u_{2}|^{2}+|v_{1}-v_{2}|^{2}\big)

on the compact set {(u,v)∈𝐑2:max⁡(|u|,|v|)≤R}\{(u,v)\in\mathbf{R}^{2}\,:\,\max(|u|,|v|)\leq R\}.

Let’s write zu:=u1−u2z_{u}:=u_{1}-u_{2} and zv:=v1−v2z_{v}:=v_{1}-v_{2}. One has

∂tzu−Δ⁡[(d1+p⁡(u1,v1))​zu]\displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{u}-\Delta\big[(d_{1}+p(u_{1},v_{1}))z_{u}\big] =Δ⁡[(p⁡(u1,v1)−p⁡(u2,v2))​u2],\displaystyle=\Delta\big[(p(u_{1},v_{1})-p(u_{2},v_{2}))u_{2}\big],
∂tzv−Δ⁡[(d2+q⁡(u1,v1))​zv]\displaystyle\partial_{t}z_{v}-\Delta\big[(d_{2}+q(u_{1},v_{1}))z_{v}\big] =Δ⁡[(q⁡(u1,v1)−q⁡(u2,v2))​v2].\displaystyle=\Delta\big[(q(u_{1},v_{1})-q(u_{2},v_{2}))v_{2}\big].

Now u1u_{1} and v1v_{1} are nonnegative and bounded, so that μp:=d1+p⁡(u1,v1)\mu_{p}:=d_{1}+p(u_{1},v_{1}) and μq:=d2+q⁡(u1,v1)\mu_{q}:=d_{2}+q(u_{1},v_{1}) are both bounded from above and below by positive constants. We can therefore use Lemma 1, firstly for zuz_{u}, to get the estimate

‖zu​(t,⋅)‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+∫0t∫𝐓dμp​zu2≤‖zu​(0)‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+(∫𝐓dzu​(0))2​∫0t∫𝐓dμp+∫0t∫𝐓d[(p⁡(u1,v1)−p⁡(u2,v2))​u2]2μp.\|z_{u}(t,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\mu_{p}\,z_{u}^{2}\\ \leq\|z_{u}(0)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\left(\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}z_{u}(0)\right)^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\mu_{p}+\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\frac{\displaystyle\Big[(p(u_{1},v_{1})-p(u_{2},v_{2}))u_{2}\Big]^{2}}{\mu_{p}}.

Using the definition of the common Lipschitz constant LR\textnormal{L}_{R} and the fact that p∈𝐑+​[X]p\in\mathbf{R}_{+}[X], with U1∈CR+U_{1}\in\textnormal{C}_{R}^{+} and |u2|≤δ|u_{2}|\leq\delta, we have for t≤Tt\leq T,

‖zu​(t,⋅)‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+∫0t∫𝐓dd1​zu2≤‖zu​(0)‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+(∫𝐓dzu​(0))2​T​(d1+p⁡(R,R))+LR2​δ2d1​∫0t∫𝐓d(zu2+zv2).\|z_{u}(t,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}d_{1}\,z_{u}^{2}\\ \leq\|z_{u}(0)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\left(\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}z_{u}(0)\right)^{2}T(d_{1}+p(R,R))+\frac{\textnormal{L}_{R}^{2}\delta^{2}}{d_{1}}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}(z_{u}^{2}+z_{v}^{2}).

A similar computation leads to an analogous estimate for zvz_{v}:

‖zv​(t,⋅)‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+∫0t∫𝐓dd2​zv2≤‖zv​(0)‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+(∫𝐓dzv​(0))2​T​(d2+q⁡(R,R))+LR2​δ2d2​∫0t∫𝐓d(zu2+zv2).\|z_{v}(t,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}d_{2}\,z_{v}^{2}\\ \leq\|z_{v}(0)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\left(\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}z_{v}(0)\right)^{2}T(d_{2}+q(R,R))+\frac{\textnormal{L}_{R}^{2}\delta^{2}}{d_{2}}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}(z_{u}^{2}+z_{v}^{2}).

The smallness assumption (17) on δ\delta ensures that

Cδ:=inf[(d1−LR2​δ2d1−LR2​δ2d2),(d2−LR2​δ2d1−LR2​δ2d2)]>0.\displaystyle\textnormal{C}_{\delta}:=\inf\bigg[\left(d_{1}-\frac{\textnormal{L}_{R}^{2}\delta^{2}}{d_{1}}-\frac{\textnormal{L}^{2}_{R}\delta^{2}}{d_{2}}\right),\left(d_{2}-\frac{\textnormal{L}_{R}^{2}\delta^{2}}{d_{1}}-\frac{\textnormal{L}^{2}_{R}\delta^{2}}{d_{2}}\right)\bigg]>0.

Summing the estimates on zu​(t,⋅)z_{u}(t,\cdot) and zv​(t,⋅)z_{v}(t,\cdot), we infer

‖(zu,zv)​(t,⋅)‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+Cδ​∫0t∫𝐓d(zu2+zv2)≤‖(zu​(0),zv​(0))‖H−1​(𝐓d)2+(∫𝐓dzu​(0))2​T​(d1+p⁡(R,R))+(∫𝐓dzv​(0))2​T​(d2+q⁡(R,R)),\|(z_{u},z_{v})(t,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\textnormal{C}_{\delta}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}(z_{u}^{2}+z_{v}^{2})\\ \leq\|(z_{u}(0),z_{v}(0))\|_{\textnormal{H}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\left(\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}z_{u}(0)\right)^{2}T(d_{1}+p(R,R))\\ +\left(\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}z_{v}(0)\right)^{2}T(d_{2}+q(R,R)),

which concludes the proof. ∎

5 Some considerations on the case when the initial data are not small

In this short section, we try to explain some of the difficulties for showing existence of weak solutions to general systems of the form (1) (when d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0 are two constants, p,qp,q are two elements of 𝐑+​[X,Y]\mathbf{R}_{+}[X,Y] vanishing at (0,0)(0,0), and when periodic boundary conditions are imposed).

Let us first notice that when no Lyapunov functional is known for the system (apart from obvious ones, such as the L1\textnormal{L}^{1} norm of the two equations), no source of strong compactness for sequences of (approximated) solutions seems to appear (at least without further assumptions on p,qp,q), since the usual a priori estimates performed on classical (non cross) diffusion systems do not seem to hold.

Let us focus on a more favorable case, that is when some Lyapunov functional (also called energy in this context) is known to exist. When it is convex, we recall that the existence of weak solutions can often be obtained [6, 9, 10, 19]. However, there are cases when an energy exists, but is not convex. Such a situation has indeed been pointed out in [5], where the following example is presented:

{∂tu−Δ⁡[(1+v2)​u]=0,∂tv−Δ⁡[(1+u2)​v]=0.\left\{\begin{lgathered}\partial_{t}u-\Delta\big[(1+v^{2})u\big]=0,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta\big[(1+u^{2})v\big]=0.\end{lgathered}\right. (18)

One checks indeed that the space integral of (1+u2)​(1+v2)(1+u^{2})(1+v^{2}) (we consider here periodic boundary conditions) decays along time. More precisely, one can check that for any smooth solution, the following bound holds:

12dd​t∫𝐓d(1+u2)(1+v2)=−∫𝐓d[|∇(u(1+v2))|2+|∇(v(1+u2))|2]≤0.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}(1+u^{2})(1+v^{2})=-\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\Big[|\nabla(u(1+v^{2}))|^{2}+|\nabla(v(1+u^{2}))|^{2}\Big]\leq 0. (19)

This dissipation of the energy controls in this situation only a part of the gradients of the solution. To highlight this lack of control of the whole gradients, we present a short proposition (in which we omit the time variable) which shows the type of pathologies which could prevent strong compactness.

Proposition 3.

There exist two sequences of functions (un)n(u_{n})_{n} and (vn)n(v_{n})_{n} taking positive values on 𝐓d\mathbf{T}^{d} such that :

  • ∙\bullet

    (un)n(u_{n})_{n} and (vn)n(v_{n})_{n} are bounded in L∞​(𝐓d)\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) ;

  • ∙\bullet

    (un​(1+vn2))n(u_{n}(1+v_{n}^{2}))_{n} and (vn​(1+un2))n(v_{n}(1+u_{n}^{2}))_{n} are bounded in H1​(𝐓d)\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) ;

  • ∙\bullet

    neither (un)n(u_{n})_{n} nor (vn)n(v_{n})_{n} is relatively compact in L2​(𝐓d)\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbf{T}^{d}).

Proof.

The polynomial

P⁡(X)\displaystyle P(X) :=(X2−3​X+1)​(X3+X−3)\displaystyle:=(X^{2}-3X+1)(X^{3}+X-3)
=(X2+1)2​X−3​(X2+1)2+9​X\displaystyle=(X^{2}+1)^{2}X-3(X^{2}+1)^{2}+9X

admits (at least) two distinct positive roots: r1<r2r_{1}<r_{2}. Consider the function ψ:=𝟏(0,1/2)−𝟏(1/2,1)\psi:=\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/2)}-\mathbf{1}_{(1/2,1)}. Its 11-periodization Ψ:=∑k∈𝐙τk​ψ\Psi:=\sum_{k\in\mathbf{Z}}\tau_{k}\psi is constant on each half-integer interval (k,k+1)/2(k,k+1)/2 for k∈𝐙k\in\mathbf{Z}, alternates values 11 and −1-1 on those, so it has a vanishing integral on each integer interval (k,k+1)(k,k+1). Define for n∈𝐍⋆n\in\mathbf{N}^{\star} the function Ψn:x↦Ψ⁡(2n​x)\Psi_{n}:x\mapsto\Psi(2^{n}x) which is now constant on each dyadic interval (k,k+1)/2n+1(k,k+1)/2^{n+1} and alternates values 11 and −1-1 on those. In particular, for m<nm<n, Ψn\Psi_{n} has a vanishing integral on each dyadic interval (k,k+1)/2m+1(k,k+1)/2^{m+1}. We claim that (Ψn)n(\Psi_{n})_{n} (restricted to (0,1)(0,1)) is an orthonormal family in L2​(0,1)\textnormal{L}^{2}(0,1) : each function is certainly of norm 11 (since its takes ±1\pm 1 as value), and if m<nm<n, we can (essentially) cover (0,1)(0,1) by a finite family ℱ\mathscr{F} of dyadic intervals (k,k+1)/2m+1(k,k+1)/2^{m+1}, so that

∫01Φn​Φm=∑I∈ℱ∫IΦn​Φm,\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\Phi_{n}\Phi_{m}=\sum_{\textnormal{I}\in\mathscr{F}}\int_{\textnormal{I}}\Phi_{n}\Phi_{m},

and as noticed before, on each element of ℱ\mathscr{F}, the function Φm\Phi_{m} is constant (by definition), whereas Φn\Phi_{n} has a vanishing integral : we have Φn⟂Φm\Phi_{n}\perp\Phi_{m} in L2​(0,1)\textnormal{L}^{2}(0,1). A similar construction can be done on 𝐓d\mathbf{T}^{d}, that we still denote (hn)n(h_{n})_{n}. The sequence

vn:=r2​1+hn2+r1​1−hn2v_{n}:=r_{2}\frac{1+h_{n}}{2}+r_{1}\frac{1-h_{n}}{2}

takes therefore its values in {r1,r2}\{r_{1},r_{2}\} (so that P⁡(vn)=0P(v_{n})=0) and does not admit a subsequence converging almost everywhere. Indeed, for n≠pn\neq p, orthogonality leads to

‖vn−vp‖2=r2−r12​‖hn−hp‖2=r2−r12,\displaystyle\|v_{n}-v_{p}\|_{2}=\frac{r_{2}-r_{1}}{2}\|h_{n}-h_{p}\|_{2}=\frac{r_{2}-r_{1}}{\sqrt{2}},

which refutes the L2​(𝐓d)\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) Cauchy criterion for (any subsequence of) (vn)n(v_{n})_{n}, whereas almost everywhere convergence would imply convergence in L2​(𝐓d)\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) by dominated convergence. Letting un:=3/(1+vn2)u_{n}:=3/(1+v_{n}^{2}), the identity P⁡(vn)=0P(v_{n})=0 proves that (1+un2)​vn=3(1+u_{n}^{2})v_{n}=3, so that the two sequences (un​(1+vn2))n(u_{n}(1+v_{n}^{2}))_{n} and (vn​(1+un2))n(v_{n}(1+u_{n}^{2}))_{n} are indeed bounded in H1​(𝐓d)\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) (because they are constant). ∎

The counterexample given in Proposition 3 relies on functions unu_{n} and vnv_{n} that are rather singular (staircase functions) and this construction cannot be reproduced in a smooth setting (because of the H1​(𝐓d)\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) bound). In the context of the parabolic PDEs that we focus on, it is natural to expect more regularity for unu_{n} and vnv_{n}. Here’s another way to describe the situation at stake. If Φn:=un​(1+vn2)\Phi_{n}:=u_{n}(1+v_{n}^{2}) and Ψn:=vn​(1+un2)\Psi_{n}:=v_{n}(1+u_{n}^{2}), the assumptions of Proposition 3 imply that both (Φn)n(\Phi_{n})_{n} and (Ψn)n(\Psi_{n})_{n} are bounded in H1​(𝐓d)\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}). A direct computation shows that the identities defining these sequences are equivalent to vn=(1+un2)−1​Ψnv_{n}=(1+u_{n}^{2})^{-1}\Psi_{n} and

un​(1+un2)2+un​Ψn2−(1+un2)2​Φn=0.\displaystyle u_{n}(1+u_{n}^{2})^{2}+u_{n}\Psi_{n}^{2}-(1+u_{n}^{2})^{2}\Phi_{n}=0.

The previous equality can be written as follows:

un5+∑k=04ak,n​unk=0,\displaystyle u_{n}^{5}+\sum_{k=0}^{4}a_{k,n}u_{n}^{k}=0,

where (ak,n)n(a_{k,n})_{n} for k=0,…,4k=0,\dots,4, are five sequences of functions that are all bounded in H1​(𝐓d)\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}). This means that at each point xx, un​(x)u_{n}(x) takes its values in the set of roots of a polynomial whose coefficients (as functions of xx) are all bounded in H1​(𝐓d)\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}). In a sense, the counterexample in Proposition 3 reduces to jumps (on a vanishing scale) from one root to another one. If we add a regularity assumption on unu_{n}, this type of counterexample is not reproducible, but other pathologies may appear, especially in the case when the polynomial has multiple roots. It is possible that for a low-degree constraint, the existence of explicit formulas allows for simplification in the analysis, but in the specific case of fifth degree polynomial that we consider here, we find this issue rather intriguing.

Appendix A Duality estimates

The forthcoming duality estimate is given within a functional setting allowing its rigorous use in the context of (very) weak solutions.

Lemma 2.

Under the assumptions of Lemma 1, if f=0f=0, zi​n∈L2​(𝐓d)z_{in}\in\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) and additionnaly μ∈Lloc∞​(𝐑+,W2,∞​(𝐓d))\mu\in\textnormal{L}_{\textnormal{loc}}^{\infty}(\mathbf{R}_{+};\textnormal{W}^{2,\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d})), then

(20)
  2. 2.

    If furthermore zi​n∈H1​(𝐓d)z_{in}\in\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}), then ∂tz∈Lloc2​(𝐑+,L2​(𝐓d))\partial_{t}z\in\textnormal{L}_{\textnormal{loc}}^{2}(\mathbf{R}_{+};\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbf{T}^{d})).

    Finally, if 0≤zi​n∈L∞​(𝐓d)0\leq z_{in}\in\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d}), then for any t≥0t\geq 0 and a.e. (s,x)∈[0,t]×𝐓d(s,x)\in[0,t]\times\mathbf{T}^{d},

    0≤z⁡(s,x)≤‖zi​n‖L∞​exp⁡(∫0t‖(Δ​μ)+​(σ)‖L∞​(𝐓d)​𝑑σ).\displaystyle 0\leq z(s,x)\leq\|z_{in}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}}\exp\left(\int_{0}^{t}\|(\Delta\mu)^{+}(\sigma)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}\,\mathrm{d}\sigma\right). (21)
Proof.

For the estimate (20), it is done for instance in [11, Corollary 19].

The case in which μ∈L∞​(0,T,W2,∞​(𝐓d))\mu\in\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(0,T;\textnormal{W}^{2,\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d})) and zi​n∈H1​(𝐓d)z_{in}\in\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) is in fact a consequence of the standard parabolic theory, because the operator −Δ⁡(μ​z)-\Delta(\mu z) may then be expanded. More precisely, we have

∂tz−μΔz−2∇z⋅∇μ−zΔμ=0,\displaystyle\partial_{t}z-\mu\Delta z-2\nabla z\cdot\nabla\mu-z\Delta\mu=0,

and the announced regularity is recovered by multiplying this equation by −Δ​z-\Delta z and performing the usual estimates (integrations by parts and use of Young’s inequality).

Appendix B Bootstrap lemma

Lemma 3.

Fix P∈𝐑+​[X]P\in\mathbf{R}_{+}[X] such that P⁡(0)=P′​(0)=0P(0)=P^{\prime}(0)=0. Then there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that, for any continuous map λ:𝐑+→𝐑+\lambda:\mathbf{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbf{R}_{+}

λ≤δ/2+P⁡(λ)⟹λ<δ.\lambda\leq\delta/2+P(\lambda)\Longrightarrow\lambda<\delta.
Proof.

Simply choose δ\delta such that 0<x≤δ⇒P⁡(x)<x/20<x\leq\delta\Rightarrow P(x)<x/2. This definition together with the inequality satisfied by λ\lambda ensure the set equality {λ≤δ}={λ<δ}\{\lambda\leq\delta\}=\{\lambda<\delta\}. The previous set is therefore closed, open and non-empty, and so it equals 𝐑+\mathbf{R}_{+}. ∎

Appendix C Estimates for the heat kernel

In this section, we recall some classical results about the heat kernel (on the torus 𝐓d\mathbf{T}^{d}). We recall that we denote QT:=[0,T]×𝐓dQ_{T}:=[0,T]\times\mathbf{T}^{d}.

We start with the Maximal regularity result for the heat flow, here in the context of the torus:

Theorem 4.

For any 1<k<+∞1<k<+\infty, m>0m>0 and φ∈𝒞∞​(𝐑+×𝐓d)\varphi\in\mathscr{C}^{\infty}(\mathbf{R}_{+}\times\mathbf{T}^{d}) vanishing at t=0t=0, one has

m∥Δφ∥Lk​(QT)≲k,d∥∂tφ−mΔφ∥Lk​(QT).\displaystyle m\|\Delta\varphi\|_{\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T})}\lesssim_{k,d}\|\partial_{t}\varphi-m\Delta\varphi\|_{\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T})}.

We then write down a classical semigroup property for the heat kernel, once again in the context of the torus:

Theorem 5.

For any k>1+d2k>1+\frac{d}{2}, any Φ∈𝒞∞​(𝐑+×𝐓d)\Phi\in\mathscr{C}^{\infty}(\mathbf{R}_{+}\times\mathbf{T}^{d}), and any m,T>0m,T>0, one has

∥Φ∥L∞​(QT)≲m,k,d∥Φ(0)∥∞+∥∂tΦ−mΔΦ∥Lk​(QT)+sups∈[0,T]|∫𝐓dΦ(s)|.\displaystyle\|\Phi\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(Q_{T})}\lesssim_{m,k,d}\|\Phi(0)\|_{\infty}+\|\partial_{t}\Phi-m\Delta\Phi\|_{\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T})}+\sup_{s\in[0,T]}\left|\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\Phi(s)\right|.

Theorems 4 and 5 are classical results in the case of the whole space or in the case of a smooth domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions (with a slightly different statement). We briefly explain below how they can be obtained in the case considered here (flat dd-dimensional torus).

We start with Theorem 4. By homogeneity, it is sufficient to treat the case m=1m=1. The equation ∂tφ−Δ​φ=F\partial_{t}\varphi-\Delta\varphi=F translates, in the (space-time) Fourier variables, as i​τ​φ^+|ξ|2​φ^=F^i\tau\widehat{\varphi}+|\xi|^{2}\widehat{\varphi}=\widehat{F}. In particular, the map F↦Δ​φF\mapsto\Delta\varphi is therefore the operator defined by the multiplier (τ,ξ)↦−|ξ|2i​τ+|ξ|2(\tau,\xi)\mapsto\frac{-|\xi|^{2}}{i\tau+|\xi|^{2}}, which satisfies the assumptions of the Mikhlin-Hörmander theorem. For more details (written in the case of the whole space 𝐑d\mathbf{R}^{d}), we refer for example to [25, Appendix D.5].

For Theorem 5, we give some more details. Since we are going to use a dyadic decomposition of the Fourier modes, we define for m∈𝐍⋆m\in\mathbf{N}^{\star}:

Cm:={k∈𝐙d:m≤|k|<2​m},Vm:=Span​{x↦ei​k⋅x:k∈Cm}.\textnormal{C}_{m}:=\{k\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}\,:\,m\leq|k|<2m\},\qquad\textnormal{V}_{m}:=\textnormal{Span}\{x\mapsto e^{ik\cdot x}\,:\,k\in\textnormal{C}_{m}\}.

We recall first the

Lemma 4 (Bernstein).

For m∈𝐍⋆m\in\mathbf{N}^{\star}, k∈[1,+∞)k\in[1,+\infty), f∈Vmf\in\textnormal{V}_{m}, one has ‖f‖∞≲(2​m)dk​‖f‖k\|f\|_{\infty}\lesssim(2m)^{\frac{d}{k}}\|f\|_{k}.

It can be obtained by estimating the Lk′L^{k^{\prime}} norm of the Dirichlet kernel (on 𝐓d\mathbf{T}^{d}) and using Young’s inequality for convolutions.

We then state the

Lemma 5.

There exists c>0\textnormal{c}>0 such that, for p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], any m∈𝐍⋆m\in\mathbf{N}^{\star} and f∈Vmf\in\textnormal{V}_{m}, the following estimate holds:

∀t≥0,‖et​Δ​f‖p≲e−c​t​m2​‖f‖p.\displaystyle\forall t\geq 0,\qquad\left\|e^{t\Delta}f\right\|_{p}\lesssim e^{-\textnormal{c}tm^{2}}\|f\|_{p}.

g=∑k∈𝐙dck​(g)​φ​(|k|/m)​ei​k⋅x.g=\sum_{k\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}c_{k}(g)\varphi(|k|/m)e^{ik\cdot x}.

where φt​(x):=e−t​x2​φ​(x)\varphi_{t}(x):=e^{-tx^{2}}\varphi(x), dm​φt​(x)=φt​(x/m)\mathrm{d}_{m}\varphi_{t}(x)=\varphi_{t}(x/m), and for any test function ψ∈𝒟⁡(𝐑)\psi\in\mathscr{D}(\mathbf{R}),

ψwidecheck​(x):=∑k∈𝐙dψ⁡(|k|)​ei​k⋅x,\widecheck{\psi}(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\psi(|k|)e^{ik\cdot x},

so that here

dm​φtwidecheck(x):=∑k∈𝐙dφ(|k|/m)e−t|k|2/m2ei​k⋅x.\widecheck{\mathrm{d}_{m}\varphi_{t}}(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\varphi(|k|/m)e^{-t|k|^{2}/m^{2}}e^{ik\cdot x}.

Thanks to Young’s inequality for convolutions, we only need to prove

‖dm​φtwidecheck‖1≲e−c​t.\|\widecheck{\mathrm{d}_{m}\varphi_{t}}\|_{1}\lesssim e^{-\textnormal{c}t}.

This can be checked using [15, Lemma 1.1], from which we can extract the following result: For any ψ∈𝒟⁡(𝐑)\psi\in\mathscr{D}(\mathbf{R}) and m∈𝐍⋆m\in\mathbf{N}^{\star}, ‖dm​ψwidecheck‖1≲‖ψ′′‖∞\|\widecheck{\mathrm{d}_{m}\psi}\|_{1}\lesssim\|\psi^{\prime\prime}\|_{\infty}.

In the particular case of ψ=φt\psi=\varphi_{t}, since φ\varphi vanishes away from 00, one has ‖φt′′‖∞≲e−c​t\|\varphi_{t}^{\prime\prime}\|_{\infty}\lesssim e^{-\textnormal{c}t} and the estimate follows. ∎

We infer from the two previous estimates the following one, for the heat flow generated by a source term in Vm\textnormal{V}_{m}.

Lemma 6.

For T>0T>0, m∈𝐍⋆m\in\mathbf{N}^{\star}, k∈[1,+∞)k\in[1,+\infty) and f∈Lk​(QT)f\in\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T}) such that f⁡(t,⋅)∈Cmf(t,\cdot)\in\textnormal{C}_{m} for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], we have the following estimate:

‖∫0te(t−s)​Δf(s)ds‖L∞​(QT)≲dmdk−2k′∥f∥Lk​(QT).\displaystyle\left\|\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(Q_{T})}\lesssim_{d}m^{\frac{d}{k}-\frac{2}{k^{\prime}}}\|f\|_{\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T})}.
Proof.

For t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and x∈𝐓dx\in\mathbf{T}^{d} we have, using Bernstein’s Lemma 4,

|∫0te(t−s)​Δ​f​(s,x)​𝑑s|≤∫0t‖e(t−s)​Δ​f​(s)‖∞​𝑑s≤(2​m)dk​∫0t‖e(t−s)​Δ​f​(s)‖k​𝑑s.\displaystyle\left|\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s,x)\,\mathrm{d}s\right|\leq\int_{0}^{t}\|e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s)\|_{\infty}\,\mathrm{d}s\leq(2m)^{\frac{d}{k}}\int_{0}^{t}\|e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s)\|_{k}\,\mathrm{d}s.

Now using the decay of the heat flow given in Lemma 5, we infer

|∫0te(t−s)​Δ​f​(s,x)​𝑑s|≤∫0t‖e(t−s)​Δ​f​(s)‖∞​𝑑s≤(2​m)dk​∫0te−(t−s)​4​c​m2​‖f⁡(s)‖k​𝑑s,\displaystyle\left|\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s,x)\,\mathrm{d}s\right|\leq\int_{0}^{t}\|e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s)\|_{\infty}\,\mathrm{d}s\leq(2m)^{\frac{d}{k}}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-(t-s)4\textnormal{c}m^{2}}\|f(s)\|_{k}\,\mathrm{d}s,

and the estimate follows directly from Hölder’s inequality. ∎

We now can prove the following

Proposition 4.

Fix T>0T>0, k>1+d2k>1+\frac{d}{2}. For all f∈Lk​(QT)f\in\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T}) having a vanishing mean at all times, one has

‖∫0te(t−s)​Δf(s)ds‖L∞​(QT)≲d,k∥f∥Lk​(QT).\displaystyle\left\|\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(Q_{T})}\lesssim_{d,k}\|f\|_{\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T})}.

Before starting the proof, we introduce a few notations related to the Littlewood-Paley decomposition for elements defined on the torus 𝐓d\mathbf{T}^{d}. Any f∈𝒟′​(𝐓d)f\in\mathscr{D}^{\prime}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) decomposes uniquely as

f:=∑k∈𝐙dck​(f)​ei​k⋅x.\displaystyle f:=\sum_{k\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}c_{k}(f)e^{ik\cdot x}.

For j∈𝐍j\in\mathbf{N}, we introduce the corresponding dyadic block

fj:=∑k∈C2jck​(f)​ei​k⋅x.\displaystyle f_{j}:=\sum_{k\in\textnormal{C}_{2^{j}}}c_{k}(f)e^{ik\cdot x}.

If ff has zero mean (that is, c0​(f)=0c_{0}(f)=0), we have (at least in 𝒟′​(𝐓d)\mathscr{D}^{\prime}(\mathbf{T}^{d}))

f=∑j∈𝐍fj,\displaystyle f=\sum_{j\in\mathbf{N}}f_{j},

and this decomposition is orthogonal in L2​(𝐓d)\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) if ff belongs to this space. We first state a result about a norm (which is actually of Besov type) which naturally appears when dealing with the previous decomposition:

Lemma 7.

For k∈[2,+∞]k\in[2,+\infty] and f∈Lk​(𝐓d)f\in\textnormal{L}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) having a vanishing mean, introducing the sequence bf:=(‖fj‖k)j∈𝐍b_{f}:=(\|f_{j}\|_{k})_{j\in\mathbf{N}}, one has

∥bf∥ℓk​(𝐍)≲k∥f∥k.\|b_{f}\|_{\ell^{k}(\mathbf{N})}\lesssim_{k}\|f\|_{k}.
Proof.

For k=2k=2 there is in fact (up to some constant) equality: this is simply Parseval’s Theorem together with the orthogonality of the dyadic blocks. For k=+∞k=+\infty, the inequality holds thanks to the continuity of f↦fjf\mapsto f_{j} from L∞​(𝐓d)\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d}) to itself, with a norm uniformly bounded w.r.t.j∈𝐍\,j\in\mathbf{N}. All the intermediate cases follow then from Riesz-Thorin interpolation Theorem. ∎

Proof of Propositon 4.

We use the Littlewood-Paley decomposition on f⁡(s)f(s) at each time s∈[0,T]s\in[0,T] to infer

∫0te(t−s)​Δ​f​(s)​𝑑s=∑j∈𝐍∫0te(t−s)​Δ​fj​(s)​𝑑s.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s=\sum_{j\in\mathbf{N}}\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}f_{j}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s.

Using the triangular inequality and the estimate of Lemma 6 for the heat flow generated by a source supported on an annulus, we get

‖∫0te(t−s)​Δ​f​(s)​𝑑s‖L∞​(QT)≲∑j∈𝐍d⁡(2j)dk−2k′​‖fj‖Lk​(QT).\displaystyle\left\|\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(Q_{T})}\lesssim_{d}\sum_{j\in\mathbf{N}}(2^{j})^{\frac{d}{k}-\frac{2}{k^{\prime}}}\|f_{j}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T})}.

The assumption k>1+d2k>1+\frac{d}{2} is equivalent to dk−2k′<0\frac{d}{k}-\frac{2}{k^{\prime}}<0, so that we get by Hölder’s inequality the estimate

‖∫0te(t−s)​Δf(s)ds‖L∞​(QT)≲d,k(∑j∈𝐍∥fj∥Lk​(QT)k)1/k,\displaystyle\left\|\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(Q_{T})}\lesssim_{d,k}\left(\sum_{j\in\mathbf{N}}\|f_{j}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T})}^{k}\right)^{1/k},

and the conclusion eventually follows from Lemma 7. ∎

We end the proof of Theorem 5 by using Proposition 4.

Proof of Theorem 5.

Introducing Φ~:=Φ−et​Δ​Φ​(0)\widetilde{\Phi}:=\Phi-e^{t\Delta}\Phi(0) and f:=∂tΦ−Δ​Φf:=\partial_{t}\Phi-\Delta\Phi, we have in particular

Φ~=∫0te(t−s)​Δ​f​(s)​𝑑s.\widetilde{\Phi}=\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s.

For a function φ\varphi on the torus, we introduce the notation

φ¯:=φ−∫𝐓dφ,\underline{\varphi}:=\varphi-\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\varphi,

with an obvious extension for functions depending also on the time variable. We therefore have

Φ¯~=∫0te(t−s)​Δ​f⁡(s)¯​𝑑s.\displaystyle\underline{\widetilde{\Phi}}=\int_{0}^{t}e^{(t-s)\Delta}\underline{f(s)}\,\mathrm{d}s.

Using Proposition 4, we infer for k>1+d2k>1+\frac{d}{2}

∥Φ¯~∥L∞​(QT)≲k,d∥f¯∥Lk​(QT)≲∥f∥Lk​(QT).\displaystyle\|\underline{\widetilde{\Phi}}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(Q_{T})}\lesssim_{k,d}\|\underline{f}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T})}\lesssim\|f\|_{\textnormal{L}^{k}(Q_{T})}.

On the other hand, we have

Φ¯=et​Δ​Φ​(0)¯+Φ¯~,\displaystyle\underline{\Phi}=\underline{e^{t\Delta}\Phi(0)}+\underline{\widetilde{\Phi}},

and the maximum principle for the heat equation implies the bound

‖et​Δ​Φ​(0)¯‖L∞​(QT)≤2​‖Φ⁡(0)‖∞,\displaystyle\|\underline{e^{t\Delta}\Phi(0)}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(Q_{T})}\leq 2\|\Phi(0)\|_{\infty},

so that the announced estimate follows. ∎

Appendix D Classical SKT system: another method yielding global uniform a priori estimates

In this short part of the Appendix, we propose another method enabling to obtain a global uniform estimate for solutions to the SKT system, which uses standard Sobolev norms. This method could be adapted to the general case of systems like (1), but since it involves taking many derivatives, we have chosen to write it in the specific case when pp and qq are both linear, that is in the case of the classical SKT system (without reaction terms):

{∂tu−Δ⁡[(d1+a1​u+b1​v)​u]=0,∂tv−Δ⁡[(d2+a2​u+b2​v)​v]=0,\left\{\begin{lgathered}\partial_{t}u-\Delta\big[(d_{1}+a_{1}u+b_{1}v)u\big]=0,\\ \partial_{t}v-\Delta\big[(d_{2}+a_{2}u+b_{2}v)v\big]=0,\end{lgathered}\right. (22)

where ai,bi,dia_{i},b_{i},d_{i} are nonnegative constants. In the sequel, for any function ff defined on 𝐓d\mathbf{T}^{d}, we use the following notation

f¯:=f−∫𝐓df.\underline{f}:=f-\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}f.
Proposition 5.

For k>d/2k>d/2, there exists δ>0\delta>0 depending on the coefficients ai,bi,dia_{i},b_{i},d_{i} and on k,dk,d, such that any smooth nonnegative solution (u,v)(u,v) to (22) satisfying

∥u¯(0),v¯(0)∥Hk​(𝐓d)≤δ/2,\displaystyle\|\underline{u}(0),\underline{v}(0)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}\leq\delta/2,

satisfies furthemore

∥u¯(t),v¯(t)∥Hk​(𝐓d)+12∫0t∥u¯(s),v¯(s)∥Hk+1​(𝐓d)2ds≤δ,\displaystyle\|\underline{u}(t),\underline{v}(t)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\|\underline{u}(s),\underline{v}(s)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k+1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\leq\delta,

for all positive time tt. In particular, due to the Sobolev embedding Hk​(𝐓d)↪L∞​(𝐓d)\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})\hookrightarrow\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\mathbf{T}^{d}), this entails a global uniform bound for the solution.

Proof.

Fix α∈𝐍d\alpha\in\mathbf{N}^{d} and denote ∂α\partial^{\alpha} the corresponding (spatial) differential operator. Applying it to the first equation of (22), we get

∂t∂αu−Δ⁡[(d1+a1​u+b1​v)​∂αu]=Δ⁡[∑0<β≤αcα,β​∂β(a1​u+b1​v)​∂α−βu],\displaystyle\partial_{t}\partial^{\alpha}u-\Delta\big[(d_{1}+a_{1}u+b_{1}v)\partial^{\alpha}u\big]=\Delta\left[\sum_{0<\beta\leq\alpha}c_{\alpha,\beta}\partial^{\beta}(a_{1}u+b_{1}v)\partial^{\alpha-\beta}u\right],

where we used Leibniz formula in the r.h.s. (with the partial order βi≤αi\beta_{i}\leq\alpha_{i}, for all ii on 𝐍d\mathbf{N}^{d}). Using Lemma 1 with z=∂αuz=\partial^{\alpha}u and μ=d1+a​u+b​v\mu=d_{1}+au+bv, for all α∈𝐍d\alpha\in\mathbf{N}^{d} satisying 0<|α|≤k+10<|\alpha|\leq k+1, and taking the sum over all those multi-indices, we get

‖u¯​(t,⋅)‖Hk​(𝐓d)2+∫0t‖u¯​(s,⋅)‖Hk+1​(𝐓d)2​𝑑s≤‖u¯​(0,⋅)‖Hk​(𝐓d)2+1d1​∑0<|α|≤k+1∫0t∫𝐓d[∑0<β≤αcα,β​∂β(a1​u+b1​v)​∂α−βu]2.\|\underline{u}(t,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\underline{u}(s,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k+1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\\ \leq\|\underline{u}(0,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\frac{1}{d_{1}}\sum_{0<|\alpha|\leq k+1}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}\left[\sum_{0<\beta\leq\alpha}c_{\alpha,\beta}\partial^{\beta}(a_{1}u+b_{1}v)\partial^{\alpha-\beta}u\right]^{2}.

A similar estimate holds for vv, and summing both, we get for U¯:=(u¯,v¯)\underline{U}:=(\underline{u},\underline{v}) (and for a symbol ≲\lesssim which depends only on the parameters ai,bi,dia_{i},b_{i},d_{i}):

‖U¯​(t,⋅)‖Hk​(𝐓d)2−‖U¯​(0,⋅)‖Hk​(𝐓d)2+∫0t‖U¯​(s,⋅)‖Hk+1​(𝐓d)2​𝑑s≲∑0<|α|≤k+1∑β+γ=α0<|β|∫0t∫𝐓d|∂βU|2⋅|∂γU|2≲∑0<|α|≤k+1∫0t∫𝐓d|∂αU|2⋅|U|2+∑0<|α|≤k+1∑β+γ=α0<|β|,|γ|<|α|∫0t∥∂βU¯(s)∥2​p2∥∂γU¯(s)∥2​p′2ds,\|\underline{U}(t,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}-\|\underline{U}(0,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\underline{U}(s,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k+1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\\ \lesssim\sum_{0<|\alpha|\leq k+1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta+\gamma=\alpha\\ 0<|\beta|\end{subarray}}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}|\partial^{\beta}U|^{2}\cdot|\partial^{\gamma}U|^{2}\\ \lesssim\sum_{0<|\alpha|\leq k+1}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbf{T}^{d}}|\partial^{\alpha}U|^{2}\cdot|U|^{2}\\ +\sum_{0<|\alpha|\leq k+1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta+\gamma=\alpha\\ 0<|\beta|,|\gamma|<|\alpha|\end{subarray}}\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial^{\beta}\underline{U}(s)\|_{2p}^{2}\|\partial^{\gamma}\underline{U}(s)\|_{2p^{\prime}}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s, (23)

for any pair of conjugate exponents 1≤p,p′≤∞1\leq p,p^{\prime}\leq\infty. In the final r.h.s., all the terms of the first sum are bounded by

sups∈[0,t]‖U¯​(s)‖∞2​∫0t‖U¯​(s)‖Hk+1​(𝐓d)2​𝑑s.\displaystyle\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\|\underline{U}(s)\|_{\infty}^{2}\,\int_{0}^{t}\|\underline{U}(s)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k+1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s.

Our goal is to obtain a similar bound for the double sum appearing on the last line. In order to do so, we will use the Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev interpolation inequality. For 0<|β|<|α|0<|\beta|<|\alpha|, this estimate implies

∥∂βf∥2​|α||β|≲d,|α|,|β|∥D|α|f∥2|β||α|∥f∥∞1−|β||α|,\displaystyle\|\partial^{\beta}f\|_{2\frac{|\alpha|}{|\beta|}}\lesssim_{d,|\alpha|,|\beta|}\|\textnormal{D}^{|\alpha|}f\|_{2}^{\frac{|\beta|}{|\alpha|}}\|f\|_{\infty}^{1-\frac{|\beta|}{|\alpha|}},

since

|β|2​|α|=|β|d+|β||α|​(12−|α|d).\displaystyle\frac{|\beta|}{2|\alpha|}=\frac{|\beta|}{d}+\frac{|\beta|}{|\alpha|}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{|\alpha|}{d}\right).

Now, getting back to the last double sum of (23), if β≠0\beta\neq 0 is linked to γ≠0\gamma\neq 0 through β+γ=α\beta+\gamma=\alpha, the conjugate of p=|α||β|p=\frac{|\alpha|}{|\beta|} is p′=|α||γ|p^{\prime}=\frac{|\alpha|}{|\gamma|}. We have therefore the following estimate for any |α|≤k+1|\alpha|\leq k+1:

∫0t‖∂βU¯​(s)‖2​p2​‖∂γU¯​(s)‖2​p′2​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial^{\beta}\underline{U}(s)\|_{2p}^{2}\|\partial^{\gamma}\underline{U}(s)\|_{2p^{\prime}}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s ≲∫0td,k⁡‖D|α|​U¯​(s)‖22​‖U¯​(s)‖∞2​𝑑s\displaystyle\lesssim_{d,k}\int_{0}^{t}\|\textnormal{D}^{|\alpha|}\underline{U}(s)\|_{2}^{2}\|\underline{U}(s)\|_{\infty}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s
≤sups∈[0,t]‖U¯​(s)‖∞2​∫0t‖U¯​(s)‖Hk+1​(𝐓d)2​𝑑s.\displaystyle\leq\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\|\underline{U}(s)\|_{\infty}^{2}\int_{0}^{t}\|\underline{U}(s)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k+1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s.

At the end of the day, we infer from estimate (23) the following one:

‖U¯​(t,⋅)‖Hk​(𝐓d)2−‖U¯​(0,⋅)‖Hk​(𝐓d)2+∫0t‖U¯​(s,⋅)‖Hk+1​(𝐓d)2​𝑑s≲sups∈[0,t]‖U¯​(s)‖∞2​∫0t‖U¯​(s)‖Hk+1​(𝐓d)2​ds,\|\underline{U}(t,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}-\|\underline{U}(0,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\underline{U}(s,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k+1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\\ \lesssim\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\|\underline{U}(s)\|_{\infty}^{2}\,\int_{0}^{t}\|\underline{U}(s)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k+1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s,

where this time ≲\lesssim depends on the coefficients ai,bi,dia_{i},b_{i},d_{i} and also on kk and dd.

Defining

A⁡(t):=‖U¯​(t,⋅)‖Hk​(𝐓d)2+∫0t‖U¯​(s,⋅)‖Hk+1​(𝐓d)2​𝑑s,A(t):=\|\underline{U}(t,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\underline{U}(s,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{H}^{k+1}(\mathbf{T}^{d})}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s,

we see that we can write

A⁡(t)−A⁡(0)≲A​(t)2,A(t)-A(0)\lesssim A(t)^{2},

and the proof can be concluded thanks to Lemma 3 of Appendix B. ∎
